concept.name: Fisher transform
concept.definition: John Ehlers' transform (Stocks & Commodities, November 2002) that maps normalized prices through the Fisher function so the output has an approximately Gaussian distribution, producing sharper, better-defined turning points than the raw price series.
concept.intuition: Price extremes are rare and squashed on a normal scale; the Fisher transform stretches the tails so that turning points stand out as crisp spikes.
concept.mechanics: Normalize price (typically the bar midpoint) to roughly -1..+1 against its n-period range with a stochastic-like step and light smoothing, then apply y = 0.5 x ln((1+x)/(1-x)); a signal line is the transform lagged one bar. Turns of the Fisher line mark candidate price reversals.
concept.formula: Fisher = 0.5 x ln((1 + X) / (1 - X)), where X is price normalized to (-1, +1) over the look-back (inputs clamped just inside +/-1).
concept.failure_modes: Sharper turning points also mean more apparent 'signals', many of which precede no real reversal; the transform assumes a bounded, mean-reverting input, so strong trends pin it at extremes.
concept.misconceptions: The Gaussian reshaping is a display transform, not evidence that prices are normally distributed or that a reversal is due; Ehlers presents it as a timing aid, not a predictor.
concept.example: If normalized X = 0.9, Fisher = 0.5 x ln(1.9/0.1) ~ 1.47 - a stretched extreme reading that flags a potential turn when it hooks down.
